title.heading: PSI
title.lead: In the autumn of 2015, smoke from forest and peatland fires (haze) covered a large part of Southeast Asia. In this game, you follow those weeks from several different positions.
rules: Every number comes from real statistics and research. Tap an underlined number to open its source.
Countries are called Country I, Country S and Country M. You can find their real names at the end, in “Data and sources”.
Numbers about deaths and children's health appear. The scenes themselves are not shown.

s_psi.label: Country S | 24-hr PSI (highest of the day)

p_pm10.label: P City | PM10 (µg/m³)
p_pm10.note: Measured against Country I's standard. It cannot simply be compared with Country S's PSI.

m_api.label: Country M, P State | API (values confirmed in news reports)
m_api.note: Days without a value confirmed in news reports show “—”.

extinguish.label: Put out the fire
extinguish.message: There is nothing you can do about it from Country S.

card.title: In a Country S housing estate

paras.text: You are a parent living in a housing estate in Country S. Your child is in the third year of primary school.
For September and October, you can spend {money} on protecting your family from the haze.
The meter at the top of the screen is Country S's air pollution index, the “24-hr PSI”. It shows the highest value recorded that day in any of five regions.
There are five bands: 0–50 Good / 51–100 Moderate / 101–200 Unhealthy / 201–300 Very unhealthy / 301 and above Hazardous.

How to play: each turn runs from a day when something happened until the day before the next event. Seeing only that day's value, you shop and set your household rules for “Unhealthy” days, then live through those days.
You won't know the later days' values until you live through them. The values are the real ones from 2015.

Your goal is to avoid as much smoke as you can while keeping an eye on both money and daily life. The points do not say whether you are a good parent; they are a yardstick for comparing different rules.

2015-09-01.story: Morning. The buildings in the distance look a little hazy.
2015-09-01.event: Country S's environment agency chief wrote to Country I for the first time to express concern about this haze.

2015-09-10.story: It is white outside the window. There is a burnt smell.
2015-09-10.event: Country S's environment minister sent a letter to Country I's minister of environment and forestry.

2015-09-14.story: Your child says their eyes are itchy.
2015-09-14.event: Country S's environment minister spoke with Country I's minister and offered again to help put out the fires.

2015-09-24.story: Just after 8 p.m. A message arrives on your phone. There will be no school tomorrow.
2015-09-24.event: At 8 p.m., the 3-hr PSI reached 317. The education ministry decided to close all primary and secondary schools the next day.

2015-09-25.story: No school today. You can barely see the block across the way.
2015-09-25.event: At 5 a.m., the 3-hr PSI reached 341. All primary and secondary schools closed because of the haze. It had never happened before.

2015-09-26.story: Saturday. You can see the block across the way better than yesterday.
2015-09-26.event: The day before, the government of Country S sent legal notices to four companies in Country I suspected of being involved in the fires.

2015-10-08.event: The highest 24-hr PSI was {psi}. The first “Moderate” day since {since}.

2015-10-19.event: The 1-hr PM2.5 concentration reached 471µg/m³, the highest 1-hour value in Country S in 2015.

2015-10-24.story: Saturday. You cancelled the weekend plans again.
2015-10-24.event: The highest 24-hr PSI was {psi}. Day {nth} this autumn in the “Very unhealthy” band or above.

2015-10-30.story: The colour outside the window is back to normal.
2015-10-30.event: The highest 24-hr PSI was {psi}. Back in the “Moderate” band.

paras.text: Country S has a “Transboundary Haze Pollution Act”, passed in {{2014|D-10}}.
Even when the fires are outside the country, companies that contribute to haze pollution in Country S can be fined up to {{S$100,000 a day|D-10}}, up to {{S$2 million in total|D-10}}.
On September 25, 2015, the government of Country S sent notices to {{four companies|D-10}} in Country I.
To send people to put out fires. To stop burning. To submit firefighting plans.
After the notices, the 24-hr PSI was still in the “Unhealthy” band or above on {{{days} days|D-01}} before the end of October.
You tried to press “Put out the fire” {tries} times.
“Put out the fire” was never pressed.

items.text: The highest 24-hr PSI in Country S in 2015 (September 25)
The highest 3-hr PSI on the same day
Days in September–October when the 24-hr PSI was in the “Unhealthy” band or above

rules.title: Rules (game settings)
lines: “Unhealthy” days (101–200) count once; “Very unhealthy” or worse (201+) count twice. “Moderate” or better counts zero.
Going out for school or shopping: {trip} ({tripMasked} with a mask).
Outdoor play: {play} ({playMasked} with a mask, 0 if you skip it, but strain +{strainSkip}).
At home: windows open {homeOpen}, closed {homeClosed} (strain +{strainClose}), closed with the air purifier {homePurifier}.
A box of masks costs {boxPrice} and lasts {box} days. An air purifier costs {purifierPrice}.
Smoke points are a way of comparing rules. They do not measure health effects, or how well masks or air purifiers really work.

outcome.title: After two months
outcome.barAll: Every precaution in the game (if money were no object)
outcome.barNote: Calculated on the real values for the same two months. Even with every precaution, smoke points do not reach zero.
outcome.whyTitle: Why it turned out this way
outcome.cMasks: Masks were used on {n} of the {bad} days that were “Unhealthy” or worse.
outcome.cPurifier: You bought an air purifier in the turn starting {date} and used it on {n} days.
outcome.cRanOut: You ran out of masks on {date}.
outcome.cDays: {{{bad} days|D-01}} were “Unhealthy” or worse, {{{very}|D-01}} of them “Very unhealthy” or worse. The smoke came from fires outside the country.
outcome.cSoldOut: Masks were sold out from September 24 to 26 (game setting).
outcome.cFloor: Under any rules, the smoke that comes into the home never reaches zero. Putting out the fires was not something a household in Country S could do.
outcome.lesson: Your rules and spending changed your smoke points. But they could not change the number of “Unhealthy” days. That was decided by fires across the border, and by the system that produces them.

card.title: On the other side of the smoke

act2.counterLabel: Acute respiratory infections (6 provinces of Country I)

paras.text: October 2015. P City, the provincial capital on K Island in Country I.
You are a family living in P City. You have a two-year-old child.
The meter at the top of the screen is P City's PM10 concentration (µg/m³). By Country I's standard, below 50 is “Good” and above 350 is “Hazardous”.
This is a different index, in different units, from Country S's 24-hr PSI in Act 1. Even on the same scale, the two cannot simply be compared.
How to play: each day is split into blocks of time. Assign them to work, looking after your child, the house and so on.
Your goal is to keep the household going for three days while protecting your family from the smoke as much as you can. Some options are not open to you.

2015-10-16.story: It is morning, but dark outside. The smell of smoke has soaked into the house.
2015-10-16.event: P City closed its schools. Counting from September, schools had been closed for at least 25 days.
2015-10-16.counter: 425,377 cases (up to October 16; 307,358 the week before)

2015-10-24.story: Your child has been coughing for three days.
2015-10-24.event: National disaster agency: more than 500,000 people in six provinces have had acute respiratory infections.

2015-10-26.story: The family next door is loading their car.
2015-10-26.event: P City's daily average PM10 has been above 1,000µg/m³ for about two weeks. Some residents are leaving town.

compare.title: The same day, in two towns
compare.note: The indices and units are different, so they cannot simply be compared side by side. Even so, this is how far the needle swung.

paras.text: According to the government of Country I, {{19 people|D-05}} died because of the haze in 2015. Another report says {{24|D-05}}.
One study estimates that the haze of September–October 2015 caused {{91,600 premature deaths|D-03}} in Country I alone.

bars.title: Deaths in Country I from the 2015 haze
bars.note: Estimates come with a range. The number changes a lot depending on the method. You will see this again at the end.

paras.text: In 2019, {{UNICEF|D-17}} pointed out that children from poor families cannot evacuate, get treatment, or buy air purifiers.

lines: A day has {blocks} blocks. Living costs {cost} money a day (food and so on).
Working outside: each block earns +{wage} money and adds +{outside} smoke points.
Indoor smoke points: {homeOpen} a day, {homeSealed} after the windows are sealed. Staying in never makes it zero.

outcome.lead: Smoke points {smoke}, money left {money}, unmet needs {unmet}.
outcome.whyTitle: Why it turned out this way

outcome.cSealed: You sealed the windows and cut the indoor smoke points.
outcome.cNotSealed: You did not seal the windows.
outcome.cHome: Even indoors, {n} smoke points built up.

outcome.cMasks: The free masks never arrived (game setting). The health ministry said it had sent {{more than 30 tonnes|D-16}} of supplies to eight provinces.
outcome.cLeave: You had no relatives to turn to (game setting). {{Some people hesitated to leave town because they had no relatives elsewhere|D-14}}.
outcome.cAir: P City's PM10 was {{1,889µg/m³|D-15}} (October 16). By Country I's standard, above 350 is “Hazardous”.
outcome.lesson: However you divided your time, smoke stayed in the home. The options most likely to cut it (an air purifier, leaving town) were never open to this family. What individual effort can change here is very small.

card.title: Who lit the fire?
card.period: In a village in Country I, in the dry season

paras.text: You are a small farmer in a village in Country I. You have to clear a new field during the dry season and plant it before the deadline.
The amounts are a unit that exists only in this game. Each time you choose a job for the week, a week passes.
{{In 9 of the 10 villages studied, fire was the only way to clear land|D-19}}.
From here, the view pulls back from your field.
The small field you cleared.
Many of the village's fields are cleared the same way. {{In 9 of the 10 villages studied, fire was the only way to clear land|D-19}}.
Around the village spread large pulpwood and oil palm concessions.

{{Fire alerts were 3–4 times denser inside concessions than outside them|D-22}} (a 2013 analysis). In central K Island, {{every year since 2001, oil palm concessions had more fire alerts than any other kind of land|D-21}}.
Under your feet is peatland. Wet peatland does not burn easily on its own. {{Much of it is drained and dried before it is set on fire|D-21}}.
{{In 2015, more than 60% of the fires in central K Island and southern S Island were on peatland|D-21}}.
{{In 2015, El Niño made the dry season last longer|D-14}}.
{{In 2015, fire alerts in central K Island and southern S Island passed 27,000. In the five years before, each province averaged about 5,500|D-21}}.

The companies that hold the concessions and invest in them are not based in just one country. {{In 2013, environmental groups found hundreds of fire hotspots on oil palm concessions held by companies from Country I, Country M, Country S and elsewhere|D-23}}.
{{In October 2026, too, a report linked concessions where fire hotspots were found to companies from several countries|D-24}}. The report says this does not directly show who set the fires.
The World Bank's analysis is that {{fire brings large economic gains to a limited group of people while harming the great majority of people in Country I|D-08}}.

{{Children exposed to the 1997 haze before birth were shorter for their age at 17|D-20}}. {{That is equivalent to a drop of about 4% in the average monthly earnings of about one million workers|D-20}}.
The children of the people who light the fires breathe that smoke too.

rules.title: Rules (game settings)
lines: You plant in the week after the field is cleared. Planting by week {deadline} gives a harvest of {full}; one week late {late1}; two or more weeks late {late2}.
Burning: {burn}. Machine: {machine} (from week {machineWeek}). The ratio, burning costing about a third of machines, is from a source (D-19); the amounts are game settings.
By hand: {hand} weeks of work on this farm. Hiring helpers ({helpers}) makes it 2 steps a week. Weeks spent clearing by hand or on a firebreak earn no outside wages (−{wage}).
Dryness: in week 1 it is too damp to burn. It gets drier every week.

When fire spreads: in parched weeks it spreads. On peatland it also spreads in dry weeks. With a firebreak, it only spreads on peatland in parched weeks. Putting out a spreading fire takes the following week (no outside wages, and planting slips).
Smoke units: {smallSmoke} if the fire burns out inside the field, {bigSmoke} if it spreads, {peatSmoke} if it gets into peat. Smoke does not cost you money. The people around you breathe it.
Your family needs {need} from this season to get through the year. Loan: +{loan}, repay {repay} after the harvest.

outcome.title: After the season
outcome.lead: {farm}: income this season {net} (needed: {need}). Smoke from your field: {smoke} units.
outcome.notMet: Not enough for your family's year.
outcome.smokeNote: Smoke units are a game count. They do not represent a real amount of smoke.
outcome.whyTitle: Why it turned out this way
outcome.c_machine: You cleared with a machine in week {week}.
outcome.c_hand: You cleared by hand and finished in week {week}.
outcome.cNone: You could not clear the field in time.
outcome.cOnTime: You planted in week {week}; the harvest was {harvest}.
outcome.cLate: Planting slipped to week {week}, and the harvest fell to {harvest}.
outcome.cEscaped: The fire spread beyond your field. The smoke and the burned land were borne by the people around you, not by you.
outcome.cRatio: {{Clearing land by burning costs about a third of clearing it with machines|D-19}}.
outcome.cDry: {{In 2015, El Niño made the dry season last longer|D-14}}.
outcome.cPeat: {{Much peatland is drained and dried before it is set on fire|D-21}}.
outcome.cMachine: Machines could only be hired from week 2 (game setting).
outcome.lesson: Burning is the cheapest and fastest. Behind that cheapness, the harm from the smoke moves to people outside the field. {{Clearing with machines is better for society as a whole|D-20}}, but {{producers are unwilling to bear that higher cost themselves|D-20}}.
outcome.tryOther: Try the other farm too, and see how the paths open to you change.

paras.text: You are in a supermarket in Japan.
Choose {min}–{max} items from the shelf to put in your basket. Then pick one product and investigate how its ingredients connect to the fires. You can make {n} checks.

basket.title: In your basket
basket.summary: Of the {n} items you chose, {m} got a mark.
basket.legend: The mark is an example of “products whose ingredients are often listed as vegetable oil or fat”. In reality it differs from product to product.

paras.text: Part of the problem is that you cannot see where, or how, things were made. With the information available now, you can neither blame any single product nor declare it unconnected.

items.text: Share of those imports from Country M and Country I
Share of food products that clearly listed palm oil as an ingredient (three supermarket chains in Europe and Australia)

pick.title: Which one will you investigate?
pick.lead: Choose one of the marked products.
pick.leadNone: None of the products in your basket got a mark. Choose one of the marked products on the shelf.

inv.title: Investigating: {product}
inv.lead: Each clue you open uses one check ({n} in all). The clues you open fill in the chain above.

chain.title: The chain
chain.contains: Product → does it contain palm oil?
chain.origin: Palm oil → which country does it come from?
chain.money: (Money) Japanese financial institutions → the palm oil sector
chain.legend: “Verified” means confirmed in a source. “Pattern” is an overall tendency. “Reported” means there is a report but not proof. “Uncertain” and “Unknown” mean the clue cannot settle it.

label.title: The label
label.text: The label on {product} just says “vegetable oil and fat”. You cannot tell from this whether it is palm oil.

imports.ask: Look up where Japan's palm oil comes from
imports.title: Import statistics
imports.text: {{Japan imports about 680,000 tonnes of palm oil a year|D-26}} (2020). {{99% of it comes from Country M and Country I|D-26}}.

maker.title: The manufacturer's reply
maker.text: The reply: “We do not disclose where our ingredients come from.” Which plantation the oil came from is unknown.

alerts.ask: Look at analysis of where fires happen
alerts.title: Fire alert analysis
alerts.text: {{Fire alerts were 3–4 times denser inside concessions than outside them|D-22}} (a 2013 analysis). But this is an overall pattern; it does not connect to the ingredients of any single product.

report.title: Environmental group report
report.text: {{In October 2026, a report linked concessions where fire hotspots were found to companies from several countries|D-24}}. The report says this does not directly show who set the fires. From this report, you cannot trace the ingredients of {product}.

finance.title: Finance investigation
finance.text: {{Japanese financial institutions lent US$6.2 billion to the palm oil sector in Southeast Asia in 2013–2019|D-28}} (an NGO investigation).

switching.title: Labelling research
switching.text: {{At three supermarket chains in Europe and Australia, palm oil was clearly listed on 7.9% of about 1,600 food products|D-27}}. {{Even counting oils with vague labels, it was at most about 40%|D-27}}. {{The same study points out that switching from palm oil to another oil does not solve the problem; it only moves it elsewhere|D-27}}.

end.title: Conclusion
end.lead: What is your conclusion about {product} and the fires that caused the haze?

options.probable: If {product} contains palm oil, the oil most likely came from Country M or Country I. But a link to specific fires cannot be shown.
options.none: {product} has nothing to do with the fires.
options.insufficient: There is not enough evidence to say anything.

verdict.overclaims: Claims more than the evidence shows

caused.overclaims: None of the clues trace the product to a specific plantation (the “country → plantation” link is unknown). There is not enough evidence to call it the cause.

probable.fits: The import statistics (D-26) support the link as far as the country. You also stated the limit clearly: it cannot be traced to specific fires.
probable.unsupported: The conclusion itself is plausible, but you did not look up where the oil comes from, so your own evidence does not support it.

none.contradicted: The clues you found (import statistics, analysis of where fires happen) show a connection at the level of countries and the sector. You cannot say there is no connection.
none.unsupported: You have no clue that shows there is no connection either. Not having checked is not evidence that something isn't there.

insufficient.fits: Your clues could not settle any of the links. “We don't know” is an honest conclusion.
insufficient.partly: For this product, that is true. But you did verify connections at the level of countries and the sector (where the oil comes from, more fires inside concessions). The evidence is missing between the product and the fires, not for the whole question.

open.contains: Does this product contain palm oil?
open.origin: Which country did this product's oil come from?
open.plantation: Which plantation or concession produced it?
open.fires: Were there fires on that plantation or concession? Who set them?

bars.title: Estimated premature deaths from the haze of September–October 2015
bars.note: These are model estimates. The total for the three countries is {{100,300|D-03}}. In this estimate, {{9 in 10|D-03}} were people in Country I.

paras.text: {{Another study estimates 6,153–17,270 deaths from short-term effects during the fires alone|D-04}} (central value {{11,880|D-04}}).
{{In that study, 69 million people in the three countries were exposed to unhealthy air|D-04}}.
The numbers change a lot depending on how the estimate is made.
{{Country I's economic losses were US$16.1 billion, about 2% of GDP|D-08}}. {{About 2.6 million hectares burned, about four times the size of B Island|D-08}}.
{{On 26 days in September–October, Country I's daily greenhouse gas emissions were higher than the daily emissions of the entire US economy|D-09}}.

epilogue.lead: This is not a story about the past.
epilogue.past: {{In September 2019, in Country M, 2,459 schools closed in areas where the Air Pollution Index (API) went above 200, affecting about 2 million students|D-18}}.

items.D-30: Fire hotspots on K Island and S Island in Country I: {hotspots}. The most since 2015 ({hotspots2015}).
items.D-31: {cases} cases of acute respiratory infection in {provinces} provinces of Country I. Of these, {under5} ({share}) were children aged five and under.
items.D-32: In Country I, {area} burned from January to the end of August. {vs2019} more than the same period in 2019.
items.D-33: Country S's 24-hr PSI reached {psi}, the highest this year (central region). On the same day, schools closed in several states of Country M.
items.D-34: Country S began subsidising medical costs for haze-related illness. The last time this was done was in 2015.
items.D-35: Ten years after 2015. An analysis finds that the ability to put out fires once they start has improved, but the incentives to burn and the weak systems for preventing fires remain.

sourcesScreen.title: Data and sources
sourcesScreen.lead: The sources for the numbers in the game. Here, the names of countries and organisations and the titles of documents are shown as they appear in the originals.
sourcesScreen.licenceD01: Contains information from Historical 24-hr PSI accessed on {date} from data.gov.sg which is made available under the terms of the Singapore Open Data Licence version 1.0
sourcesScreen.licenceD02: D-02 (Monthly Air Pollution, OpenDOSM) is published under CC BY 4.0. This game does not use its numbers.
sourcesScreen.checkLang: The check notes were written in Japanese and translated.
sourcesScreen.assumptionsLead: The following are not real data. They are settings that move the game along.
assumptions: Act 1: the family, the money for haze protection (S$300), the prices of masks and the air purifier, how many days a box lasts, the days masks are sold out, not being eligible for the free masks, and how smoke points and strain are counted (only the daily 24-hr PSI values are real, from D-01)
Act 2: the family, the blocks of time in a day, the money units, income and costs, smoke points, not being able to buy an air purifier, the free masks not arriving, and having no relatives elsewhere

Act 3: the two farms, the money in hand, the weeks and the deadline, dryness, when fire spreads, the harvest and the money the family needs, the loan, and smoke units (only the ratio of about 1/3 between burning and machines is a number from D-19)
Act 4: the products on the shelf and the palm oil mark, the number of checks, the label wording and the manufacturer's reply (the other clues come from sources)
Act 5: the setting of a person living in P State, and the story text. The “based on an interview” text paraphrases the words of a person living in P State
All story text (the parts marked “Game setting”) is fiction

card.title: Smoke that should be far away

paras.text: October 2026. P State, Country M.
You are a person living in P State.
The meter at the top of the screen is Country M's Air Pollution Index (API). It only shows P State values confirmed in news reports.
There are five bands: 0–50 Good / 51–100 Moderate / 101–200 Unhealthy / 201–300 Very unhealthy / above 300 Hazardous.

2026-10-01.story: In the morning, you read the news on your phone. Across the sea, forests and peatland are burning.
2026-10-01.event: The API was “Unhealthy” in 8 places on the peninsula of Country M (10 a.m.).

close.label: Close the news
close.result: Outside the window, it is the usual sky.

read.label: Read the article to the end
read.result: It felt like something far away.

2026-10-08.story: It is white outside the window. There is a burnt smell.
2026-10-08.event: The API was “Unhealthy” in 3 places in P State. The education ministry told schools to stop outdoor activities above 100 and to close above 200.

window.label: Close the windows
window.result: You closed the windows. The air in the room smells a little too.

laundry.label: Bring the laundry in
laundry.result: The smell stayed in your shirts.

run.label: Skip your evening run
run.result: You put your shoes back by the door.

2026-10-09.story: On the news map, the band of smoke is stretching north.
2026-10-09.event: Schools closed in 6 states and territories of Country M. Schools in P State are open as usual. Areas where the API stays above 150 for 3 days in a row will close schools from the 12th.

neighbour.label: Read the news from the neighbouring country
neighbour.result: {{In Country S too, the 24-hr PSI reached 192, the highest this year|D-33}}.

check.label: Check P State's numbers again and again
check.result: The same number as a moment ago. You opened it again anyway.

2026-10-11.story: The sky is white. Rain clouds, or smoke? You can't tell.
2026-10-11.event: At 2 monitoring stations in P State, the API was back to “Good” (10 a.m.).

open.label: Try opening the window
open.result: Is that the smell of rain, or of smoke? You can't tell.

app.label: Look at the number in the app
app.result: The number is in the “Good” band. The sky is still white.

2026-10-13.story: You open the news again. The numbers have gone up.
2026-10-13.event: Fire hotspots on K Island and S Island in Country I reached 38,511. The most since 2015.

close.label: Close the app
close.result: Even as you closed it, you felt you would open it again.

send.label: Send the news to your family

2026-10-15.story: You have started keeping masks by the front door.
2026-10-15.event: The API was below 150 at all stations in P State (2 p.m.). Classes on the 16th will run as usual, but outdoor activities are postponed and masks are recommended.

mask.label: Go out wearing a mask
mask.result: Some people were wearing masks, and some were not.

nomask.label: Go out without a mask
nomask.result: On the way, you wondered whether to turn back.

paras.text: Every day, you read the news. You check the numbers. You look up at the sky.
“The clean air is being polluted. I can't tell whether what I'm seeing now is rain or haze.”
